content: Herpangina is a viral illness characterized by the formation of ulcers and sores (lesions) inside the mouth, accompanied by a sore throat and fever. Symptoms of Herpangina: Patients often experience fever. Headaches are a common symptom. There may be a noticeable loss of appetite. A sore throat or painful swallowing is frequently reported. Ulcers typically develop in the mouth and throat. Similar sores may also appear on the feet, hands, and buttocks. These ulcers usually have a white to whitish-gray base surrounded by a red border. The ulcers can be extremely painful. Generally, only a few sores are present. Causes of Herpangina: Herpangina is most commonly caused by Coxsackie group A viruses. High-Risk Groups: While the exact number of herpangina cases is unknown, it is a common childhood infection. It is most frequently observed in children aged 3 to 10 years, though it can occur in individuals of any age. The likelihood of developing herpangina increases if there are cases in the child’s school or neighborhood. Diagnosis: Diagnostic tests are usually unnecessary. The diagnosis is typically made based on the patient’s medical history and findings from a physical examination. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care: Contact your healthcare provider if: Fever, sore throat, or mouth sores persist for more than five days. Your child has difficulty drinking fluids or shows signs of dehydration. The fever becomes very high or does not subside. Treatment Options: Treatment focuses on managing symptoms: Use acetaminophen (Tylenol) or ibuprofen (Motrin) for fever and discomfort, as recommended by your doctor. Increase fluid intake, particularly cold milk products. Gargling with cool water or consuming popsicles may provide relief. Avoid hot beverages and citrus fruits. Follow a non-irritating diet. Cold milk products, including ice cream, are often the best choices during a herpangina infection. Avoid fruit juices, as they are too acidic and may irritate mouth sores. Spicy, fried, or hot foods should also be avoided. Topical anesthetics for the mouth, such as those containing benzocaine or xylocaine, may be used but are generally not required. Medical Care for Herpangina: Directions to hospitals treating herpangina can be sought if necessary. Prognosis: The illness typically resolves within one week. Possible Complications: Dehydration is the most common complication but can be effectively managed by a healthcare provider. Prevention of Herpangina: The Coxsackie virus is transmitted through fecal contamination, meaning the virus can be contracted by touching the mouth or eating without thoroughly washing hands. Practicing good hand hygiene can help prevent the transmission of most viruses. Being aware of other cases of herpangina in your neighborhood or school may facilitate earlier diagnosis.
